messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] deactivate - strange behaviour
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This is expected. It's not a bug, but a current limitation. This is
what happens:

- Generators are initialised at t=0, and they draw the first
interarrival times, which are dt=1 and dt=3.
- So they create new arrivals and insert them in the event queue at
t=1 (dummy0) and 3 (kukucs0) respectively.
- dummy0 is executed at t=1 and it deactivates kukucs, but note that
kukucs0 is already in the event queue.
- So kukucs0 is executed at t=3.

I think it's not a great issue, but solving this limitation would
require keeping track of such arrivals to be able to cancel them, and
this would impact the overall performance. So I decided to keep the
current behaviour, unless a much bigger issue with this is
demonstrated at some point.

Iñaki

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Re: Custom log_ method
messages.body_plain:
On Sun, 27 Jan 2019 at 21:58, Erik Brakkee <erik.b...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Adding an 'env' object to the global environmnet is a work around. Is there a way in R to call a function and explicitly add a variable to the scope of a function? In that case I can explicitly pass an object named 'env' to the function that create the trajectory.

It's not a workaround, but the way to go. A simmer environment is just
a pointer to a C++ object (plus some methods to work with it), so the
only important thing is that it should be available in some parent
environment when a trajectory uses it. That's why one of our
recommended best practices (see section 4.3 in [1]) is to instantiate
the environment in the first place, e.g.,

env <- simmer()

traj <- trajectory() %>%
  log_(function() paste0("Current simulation time: ", now(env)))

env <- env %>%
  add_generator("dummy", traj, at(rexp(1, 1))) %>%
  run()

The code is more readable and some potential mistakes are avoided.

Iñaki

[1] https://r-simmer.org/articles/simmer-02-jss.pdf

project 1 starts at time 10, using 10 machine A with timeout 15 on average; using 50 machine B with timeout  5 on average;

project 3 starts at time 30, using 1000 machine A with timeout  500 on average; using 5000 machine B with timeout  100 on average

  timeout(function() rnorm(1, 15)) %>%

  seize("machine B", 50) %>%

  release("machine B", 50)

Dear Iñaki,

The purpose of this simulation is to try to maximize the usage of machine A and B.

For the same example,

There are 1000 machine A and 1000 machine B available. There are four types of projects, each type uses 100, 200, 500 and 400 machine A with different timeouts.
Project 1 (type 1) uses 100 machine A;
project 2 (type 2) uses 200 machine A;
project 3 (type 3) uses 500 machine A;
project 4 (type 4) uses 400 machine A, so project 4 will wait until project 1 finishes machine A step.
project 5 (type 2) arrives slightly later than project 4 but it is the same type as project 2, which only uses 200 machine A, so project 5 can start earlier than project 4. Project 5 can start even if project 1 is not finished, so all 1000 machine A can be utilized as many as possible each day. How do I decide which project a new arrival will follow? Each new arrival follows in one of the four types of projects. It is not completely random. I know in advance which new arrivals have which project type. How can I code this in branch? Also how can I code the above example so a later arrival can start earlier if it uses fewer machines?

Thanks so much!

 env <- simmer("machines")
env

project <- trajectory("project path") %>%

How should I specify the branch since the arrival time for each of the four project types are random?

Do you mean that you have a vector of arrival times (probably
something measured in a real setup) and you know the type for each
arrival? Then use add_dataframe instead of add_generator. See
https://www.enchufa2.es/archives/simmer-3-8-0.html

If you split your data frame in several data frames by type, then you
can feed each project trajectory individually instead of using a
branch.

> For the priority, fewer machines -> higher priority. That is true but if one project that needs more machines arrives and there are enough machines for this project, then this project will be initiated. But when there are not enough machines for this project, another project that arrives later but needs fewer machines will be initiated. How can we manage this kind of situation?

I don't see the problem. If a project that needs more machines arrives
and there are enough machines, it means that there are no other
projects with fewer machines waiting in the queue, so it will be
served. If a project with fewer machines arrives, then it will have
priority and it will be initiated.
